PAPER: BIBLIOMETRIC RESEARCH Published Online: August 13, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multirev.2026092 A bibliometric study on the role of artificial intelligence in enhancing investment decision- making processes Mfaume Ismail Mahmouda | Arni Surwantia aFaculty of Postgraduate Studies, The Doctoral Management Program (PSDM), Universitas Muhammadiyah Yogyakarta, Indonesia. Abstract The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly impacted various sectors, especially finance, where it has revolutionized how investment decisions are made. A bibliometric analysis of research publications from 2015 to 2025 highlights remarkable trends, with over half (51.7%) of all studies published in just the last two years (2024–2025), underscoring the field's explosive growth. Geographically, India has emerged as the top contributor, accounting for 28% of total publications, followed by the United States, China, and the United Kingdom. The interdisciplinary nature of AI research is evident in its subject distribution: Computer Science leads with 24.8% of publications, followed by Business & Economics (19.6%), Engineering (14.3%), Decision Sciences (12.7%), Mathematics (9.8%), and other fields making up the remaining 18.8%. AI technologies, such as machine learning and data analytics, are transforming finance by enhancing portfolio management, refining risk assessment, and enabling advanced predictive analytics. These innovations facilitate more efficient, data-driven investment strategies. Using the Scopus database and VOSviewer software, this study analyzes co- authorship patterns and keyword co-occurrence to map the field's landscape. The findings highlight key trends in AI applications for investment decision-making, particularly in algorithmic trading, risk management, and portfolio optimization. As global financial markets grow increasingly complex, AI-driven approaches offer critical support for decision- making, presenting both opportunities and challenges for researchers and practitioners. This bibliometric study sheds light on emerging trends, influential research, and significant gaps in the field. It provides valuable insights for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers seeking to understand AI's evolving role in shaping investment strategies and decision- making frameworks. Keywords: machine learning algorithms, predictive analytics, investment portfolio, risk management, data visualization 1. Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing industries by providing automated, data-driven solutions that significantly enhance decision-making processes (Nardone et al., 2024). In particular, the financial sector has experienced a paradigm shift, with AI applications increasingly influencing investment strategies, portfolio management, and risk assessment (Ghanta et al., 2024). These advanced tools, including machine learning algorithms and predictive analytics, have transformed traditional investment decision-making processes, enabling a more data-centric approach to understanding market dynamics (Shahzadi et al., 2024). As AI technologies continue to develop, they offer investors novel methodologies to optimize investment decisions, enhance portfolio management, and mitigate risks (Devapitchai et al., 2024). Ajibade et al. (2024) Argues that the growing complexity of global financial markets calls for sophisticated tools that can help investors navigate uncertainties and maximize returns. AI has emerged as a powerful solution in this regard, providing more accurate predictions and insightful analysis through advanced algorithms (Jang et al., 2024). These tools not only streamline risk assessment but also assist in identifying new investment opportunities that may have otherwise gone unnoticed. As the role of AI in the financial sector expands, it continues to influence various aspects of investment decision- making, from asset allocation to performance evaluation (Nardone et al., 2024). Given the increasing relevance of AI in finance, it is essential to assess the academic literature surrounding its applications in investment decision-making (Koo, 2024). A bibliometric study offers a comprehensive approach to mapping the intellectual structure and identifying key research trends in this evolving field (Filos, 2019). By leveraging bibliometric analysis tools such as VOSviewer, this study aims to provide insights into the influential contributions and evolving methodologies used in AI-driven investment research. Such an analysis will help identify dominant research areas, as well as emerging themes that are shaping the future of AI applications in finance (Akour et al., 2024). AI-driven tools, including machine learning algorithms, deep learning models, and predictive analytics, have enabled investors to optimize decision-making with greater accuracy and efficiency (Ajibade et al., 2024). As these technologies evolve, they are expected to refine financial modeling and forecasting further, resulting in more precise and personalized investment Multidiscip. Rev. (2026) 9:e2026092 Received: February 2, 2025 | Accepted: March 6, 2025 Mahmoud and Surwanti (2026) 2 strategies (Baklanova et al., 2023). With the growing ability to analyze large volumes of financial data in real-time, AI also allows investors to tailor strategies to individual risk profiles and preferences, fostering a more customized approach to investment management (Pattnaik et al., 2024). This bibliometric study seeks to map the current landscape of AI-driven investment research and identify future directions and research gaps in the field. By analyzing keyword co-occurrence and thematic clusters, this study aims to shed light on underexplored areas and suggest potential avenues for further inquiry. Ayaz and Zahid (2024) Suggests that understanding the bibliometric structure of AI in investment decision-making is crucial for guiding future research efforts and enhancing the practical applications of AI in finance. Ultimately, this research contributes valuable insights for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers, paving the way for more efficient financial practices and improved market outcomes. 2. Materials and methods As global financial markets grow more complex, adopting AI methodologies becomes imperative. AI applications have introduced novel approaches to economic forecasting, algorithmic trading, and automated investment advisory services (Artene et al., 2024). Given the significant role that AI plays in shaping modern financial practices, there is a need for a systematic analysis of the literature to identify key research trends, influential studies, and future directions. Bibliometric analysis is an effective tool for mapping intellectual contributions, analyzing research patterns, and assessing the evolving impact of AI on investment decision-making. This study aims to explore the following questions: RQ1: What are the research trends in AI applications for investment decision-making? RQ2: Which authors have significantly contributed to this area? RQ3: What are the dominant international research collaborations in AI-driven investment decision-making? RQ4: Which subject areas most influence AI-driven investment decision-making? RQ5: How do keyword co-occurrence patterns reveal trends and gaps in AI-driven investment research? By analyzing scholarly publications via bibliometric techniques, this study provides a structured overview of the existing body of knowledge on AI-driven investment decision-making, offering valuable insights for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers. The methodology for this study employs bibliometric analysis to review the academic literature on AI in investment decision-making systematically (Akour et al., 2024). The Scopus database, which includes peer-reviewed articles, conference proceedings, and other academic sources, collects data from 2015 to 2025. A comprehensive search strategy incorporates keywords such as "Artificial Intelligence," "Investment Decision-Making," "Machine Learning in Finance," and "AI-driven Investment Strategies." VOSviewer, a powerful tool for bibliometric analysis, is used to create network visualizations that depict author collaborations and keyword co-occurrence (van Eck & Waltman, 2017). The data was pre-processed to ensure consistency, including removing duplicates, cleaning metadata, and normalizing author and institutional names. The results offer insights into the intellectual structure and suggest future research directions. The research employed a systematic approach to collect and analyze bibliometric data, as shown in Figure 1 below. Keyword co-occurrence analysis reveals several emerging themes in AI-driven investment decision-making, as shown in Figure 7 below. Key trends include the increasing focus on machine learning, deep learning, and predictive analytics as methodologies for improving investment strategies. Other vital topics include algorithmic trading, risk management, portfolio optimization, and financial forecasting. The co-occurrence analysis indicates that terms such as "artificial intelligence," "decision making," and "investments" often appear in conjunction, signifying a significant research emphasis on the use of AI to improve financial decision-making. Numerous recent studies highlight the capacity of AI-driven models to analyze extensive financial data, hence refining investment methods, optimizing portfolio management, and augmenting predictive accuracy. The rising prominence of deep learning in this field highlights the increasing need for AI-driven methods to traverse intricate financial markets (Mergen et al., 2024). Nonetheless, the analysis reveals significant deficiencies in the literature, especially with respect to the examination of ethical implications in AI-driven investment decision-making. Although AI improves efficiency and accuracy, issues pertaining to transparency, algorithmic bias, and regulatory compliance are insufficiently examined. The scant discourse on ethical AI in financial decision-making indicates the need for additional studies on responsible AI practices, equity in algorithmic trading, and the societal ramifications of AI-driven investing methods. Rectifying these deficiencies can increase the accountability and reliability of AI applications in finance, ensuring that technical progress adheres to ethical and legal benchmarks (Alcázar-Blanco et al., 2024). Final Considerations The findings of this study highlight the rapid expansion of AI-driven investment research, with an increasing focus on machine learning, algorithmic trading, and risk management. A notable trend is the growing interest in AI applications for financial forecasting, which has led to substantial academic contributions in predictive analytics and automated trading strategies. The bibliometric analysis also reveals significant international collaborations, with leading research hubs concentrated in the United States, China, the United Kingdom, and India. These collaborations underscore the interdisciplinary nature of AI research, integrating expertise from finance, economics, computer science, and data analytics (Gu et al., 2021). Despite the extensive research on AI in finance, several critical gaps remain unaddressed. One of the most pressing concerns is the ethical implications of AI-driven investment strategies. Issues such as algorithmic bias, transparency, and regulatory compliance require further investigation to ensure the responsible deployment of AI in financial markets (Patil et al., 2024). Additionally, more research is needed to explore the implications of AI applications in emerging markets, where financial infrastructures and regulatory frameworks may differ from those in developed economies. Future research should focus on creating more interpretable AI models, integrating AI with traditional economic theories, and enhancing the robustness of algorithmic trading strategies. Addressing these gaps will contribute to a more responsible and practical application of AI in investment decision-making. This bibliometric study provides a structured overview of the evolving landscape of AI applications in investment decision-making. The findings indicate a significant rise in AI-related research driven by advances in machine learning, data analytics, and financial modeling. While AI can potentially enhance investment strategies, further research is needed to address ethical concerns, regulatory frameworks, and AI integration with traditional economic models. As AI technologies continue to advance, interdisciplinary collaboration will play a crucial role in shaping the future of AI-driven investment strategies. Researchers, practitioners, and policymakers must work together to harness AI's potential while ensuring its responsible implementation in financial markets. This study provides a foundation for future research, guiding scholars toward emerging trends and unexplored areas in AI-driven investment decision-making. JSON: Name: ai_invest_biblio_pipeline Title: Longitudinal causal bibliometric analysis using topic modeling and network inference to quantify the effect of AI methodology choice on research impact in investment decision-making Short Hypothesis: Articles on investment decision-making that explicitly use explainable AI (XAI) methods attain higher 2-year citation growth than comparable articles that do not use XAI, after controlling for publication year, venue prestige, and authors' prior citation records. Related Work: Existing bibliometric studies on AI in finance primarily apply descriptive methods: publication counts, subject-area shares, co-authorship networks, and keyword co-occurrence visualizations (often produced with VOSviewer). Prior approaches rely on single-source metadata (commonly Scopus), static snapshots, and coarse keyword matching to identify topics and methods. Topic detection has typically used keyword co-occurrence or simple LDA, and impact analysis is normally limited to aggregate citation counts or network centrality. Limitations in current work include: narrow database coverage and language bias; weak method labeling (keyword matches produce false positives/negatives); lack of longitudinal modeling of citation trajectories; absence of explicit causal inference to estimate method effects on impact (confounding by venue, year, or author prominence); limited reproducibility and parameter transparency; and insufficient attention to ethical-topic prevalence. These gaps prevent strong claims about whether adopting specific AI methodologies (e.g., XAI, deep learning) causally affects research impact in investment decision-making. Abstract: We address whether methodological choices in AI research causally influence scholarly impact within the domain of investment decision-making. We propose a reproducible bibliometric pipeline that combines metadata harvesting across multiple sources, robust method-labeling via supervised classification and topic modeling, dynamic citation-growth modeling, network centrality feature extraction, and causal-effect estimation using propensity score matching and longitudinal regression. The main contribution is an end-to-end, open analytical workflow that moves beyond descriptive co-occurrence maps to quantify the effect of using explainable-AI methods on short-term citation growth while controlling for confounders (publication year, venue prestige, author prior influence). Expected outcomes are (1) validated method-label classifier and topic map of AI-in-investment literature, (2) estimated average treatment effect of XAI adoption on 1–3 year citation growth with uncertainty bounds, and (3) an ablation analysis showing sensitivity to data sources and confounder sets. Results will inform researchers and policymakers about methodological choices that correlate with measurable scholarly influence. Experiments: Datasets: 1) Metadata export (title, abstract, keywords, authors, affiliations, references, citations, publication year, venue) from Scopus for query terms covering AI AND (investment OR portfolio OR trading OR risk) for 2015–2025. 2) Supplementary metadata from Web of Science, CrossRef, and arXiv for coverage; deduplicate via DOI. 3) Citation time series (monthly/yearly) up to 3 years post-publication. Expected sample size: all matching documents (~500–1000). Preprocessing: normalize author names, affiliation names; language filter: English; remove duplicates. Method-labeling: build a labeled seed set (n≈1000) via rule-based regex (keywords: "explainable", "XAI", "interpretable", "SHAP", "LIME") plus manual annotation; train a classifier (RoBERTa-base fine-tuned) to predict method categories {XAI, deep_learning, traditional_ML, econometric}. Validate classifier with 5-fold CV; report precision/recall/F1 for XAI label. Topic modeling: BERTopic with Sentence-BERT embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), min_topic_size=10; report topic coherence (c_v) and top topic terms. Network features: construct co-authorship and citation networks; compute degree, eigenvector centrality, betweenness, and community modularity. Baselines: (A) descriptive pipeline (VOSviewer co-occurrence and raw counts); (B) topic-model-only impact regression; (C) classification-only labeling without network features. Causal estimation: treat XAI label as binary treatment. Confounders: publication year, venue impact metric (SJR/IF proxy), authors' prior cumulative citations, country, document type. Primary estimator: propensity score matching (PSM) with logistic propensity model (include interactions), caliper=0.1, 1:1 nearest neighbor without replacement; outcome: 2-year citation growth (citations at 24 months minus citations at publication). Secondary estimators: negative binomial regression of 2-year citations with treatment and confounders; difference-in-differences for quasi-experimental adoption events; bootstrap (1000 samples) for 95% CI. Evaluation metrics: ATE with 95% CI and p-value; effect size (Cohen's d); model fit (AIC/BIC, RMSE for predictive regressions); classifier metrics (precision, recall, F1 for XAI); topic coherence (c_v); network modularity. Ablation studies: 1) remove network features from propensity model; 2) run PSM using Scopus-only vs multi-source combined data; 3) use simple keyword-based XAI label vs classifier label; 4) different propensity model specifications (random forest propensity vs logistic). Statistical significance threshold alpha=0.05. Software: Python ecosystem (pandas, scikit-learn, transformers, BERTopic, NetworkX, statsmodels), VOSviewer for comparative visual baselines. Reproducibility: provide code, seeds, and containerized environment. Risk Factors and Limitations: Coverage and selection bias: database differences (Scopus vs WoS vs CrossRef) and language filtering produce incomplete samples and geographic/language bias. Method-labeling errors: classifier misclassification (false positives/negatives) for XAI and method categories will bias effect estimates. Confounding and causal limits: unobserved confounders (e.g., novelty, funding, dataset availability, institutional prestige not captured by controls) may invalidate causal claims; PSM and regression reduce but do not eliminate bias. Temporal bias: citation accrual is time-dependent and skewed for recent publications (2024–2025) producing unstable short-horizon estimates. Name disambiguation: imperfect author disambiguation affects prior-citation controls and network measures. Measurement error: venue prestige proxies and citation counts vary across sources. Scalability and compute: full-text extraction, embedding generation, and large-network computations require substantial CPU/GPU and memory; practical limits may force sampling. Generalization: findings specific to AI-in-investment literature and to the 2015–2025 window may not generalize to other domains or future periods. Ethical: bibliometric analysis may reinforce incentives toward methods that maximize citations rather than scientific quality.
